* Respondents of color are more inclined than white respondents to believe that climate change effects are shared "equally".
* By a margin of approximately 2 to 1, respondents across all groups believe that climate change "can be stopped" rather than believing it is too late.
* There is a difference in perceived readiness for climate impacts between those in high-resource areas and those in low-income neighborhoods, with high-resource neighborhoods (which are mostly white) being more likely to see themselves as "very prepared".

The Climate Emergency Preparedness: Art x Cultural Resilience event was hosted in May [1]. During the event, the speakers held a conversation that explored the wisdom and beauty of different cultures, cultural organizing, and artistic expression in the development of resilient and sustainable communities. * Erin Genia, Artist-in-Residence, City of Boston * Meghan Venable-Thomas, Cultural Resilience Program Director, Enterprise Community Partners Kim Szeto, the Public Art Program Director at the New England Foundation for the Arts, served as the moderator.

Additionally, Patricio Belloy, a student working with Professor Stacy VanDeveer, completed an assessment of resilience planning in East Boston through a climate justice lens [2].
